deep.reconstruction:
Context (my inference, consistent with the notation): this is a draft of the proof of Disquisitiones Arithmeticae art. 40. The proposition is: if μ = gcd(A,B,C,...), there exist integers a,b,c,... with aA + bB + cC + ... = μ. The earlier, unseen step treats two numbers: λ = gcd(A,B) and integers α,β with αA + βB = λ (Bézout for two numbers, obtained via the Euclidean algorithm). This page carries out the induction step to a third number C.

(1) Let λ' = gcd(λ, C). Choose integers k, γ with kλ + γC = λ' (two-number case again).

(2) Substitute λ = αA + βB to get kαA + kβB + γC = λ'.

(3) λ' is a common divisor of A, B, C. Implicit step (mine): λ' | λ, and λ | A and λ | B, so λ' | A and λ' | B; also λ' | C by definition.

(4) λ' is the greatest common divisor. Suppose some common divisor θ > λ' existed. Divide the identity in (2) by θ: kα·(A/θ) + kβ·(B/θ) + γ·(C/θ) = λ'/θ. The left side is an integer, so λ'/θ would be an integer. But 0 < λ'/θ < 1, which is absurd (Q.E.A.). Implicitly this also shows that every common divisor of A, B, C divides λ'.

(5) Setting a = kα, b = kβ, c = γ and μ = λ' gives aA + bB + cC = μ = gcd(A,B,C), as proposed. The same step iterates for any further numbers.

The previous page is an unrelated German poem.
errors: No mathematical errors. Two steps are left implicit but are trivial and correct: λ' | λ | A,B, and positivity of λ' (needed so that 0 < λ'/θ < 1). The struck-out words 'hic ipsum λ'' are a self-correction in which Gauss renamed the hypothetical larger divisor θ.

results.what: Existence of integers a,b,c with aA+bB+cC = gcd(A,B,C), proved by iterating the two-number case: gcd(A,B,C) = gcd(gcd(A,B),C). This is a draft of the proof in Disquisitiones Arithmeticae art. 40, with identical notation (λ, λ', μ, a,b,c).
results.modern_name: Bézout's identity for several integers (extended gcd / linear combination of gcd)
results.usually_credited_to: Bachet de Méziriac (1624) for two numbers; Bézout (1779) for polynomials; the n-number form appears in Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae art. 40 (1801)

deep.surprise_reason: This is essentially the published proof of Disquisitiones Arithmeticae art. 40, notation and all. It is an elementary, well-known result, already in print under Gauss's name.

Two-number step αA+βB=λ with A=12, B=18, α=-1, β=1, λ=6
kλ+γC=λ' with λ=6, C=27, k=5, γ=-1, λ'=3
Combined identity kαA+kβB+γC=λ'=gcd(A,B,C), i.e. a=-5, b=5, c=-1 gives aA+bB+cC=μ=3
